tips.title: Four cells, half the chromosomes
tips.body: Meiosis produces **4 daughter cells**, each with **half** the number of chromosomes, and each **genetically different**. Three facts, and questions usually want all three.

tips.title: The stages of meiosis are not required
tips.body: The specification says so directly. You need the **outcome** — four genetically different haploid gametes — not prophase, metaphase and the rest. Learning the stages is time that earns nothing on this paper.

tips.title: The trade is variation against finding a mate
tips.body: **Asexual**: no mate needed and a rapid cycle, but **no variation**. **Sexual**: **variation**, but a mate must be found. Each method's advantage is the other's drawback, so learning one gives you both.

tips.title: Haploid and diploid
tips.body: **Haploid** means **half** the chromosomes — a gamete, with 23 in humans. **Diploid** means the **full** set — a body cell, with 46. Fertilisation joins two haploid gametes to make a diploid zygote.

tips.title: Meiosis makes gametes; mitosis makes copies
tips.body: **Meiosis**: 4 cells, **half** the chromosomes, **genetically different** — for gametes. **Mitosis**: 2 cells, the **full** number, **genetically identical** — for growth and repair.

why.matters:
Sexual reproduction is expensive. You have to find a mate, which costs time and energy and may fail, and you pass on only half your genes — where an organism reproducing asexually passes on all of them and needs nobody.

It survives because of what the halving buys: **variation**. Every gamete is different, so every offspring is a new combination, and a population of new combinations can survive a change that would have killed a population of clones. Meiosis is the machinery that produces the variety.

examples.title: Why the chromosome number has to halve
examples.body:
A human body cell has **46** chromosomes. If a sperm and an egg each carried 46, the child would have 92, and their children 184. Within a few generations the arithmetic is absurd.

So gametes are **haploid** — 23 each — and fertilisation puts the set back to 46. That is the whole reason meiosis exists as a second kind of division: mitosis copies, and something had to halve.

props.caption: Halve at the gamete, and fertilisation puts it back

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion showing a human body cell with forty-six chromosomes against a gamete with twenty-three, half the set, so that fertilisation restores the full number

examples.title: Two divisions that are easy to confuse and do opposite jobs
examples.body:
Both are cell division and almost nothing else about them matches. **Mitosis** makes two cells with the full set of chromosomes and identical DNA, for growth and repair. **Meiosis** makes four, each with half the set, each genetically different, and only for gametes.

The specification does not ask for the stages of meiosis — it asks for the **outcome**, which is those three facts together. If an answer has two cells, or identical ones, it has described the wrong division.

visual.alt: A table comparing mitosis, which gives two genetically identical cells with the full set of chromosomes for growth and repair, with meiosis, which gives four genetically different cells with half the set, for gametes

examples.title: Why a field of clones is a risk
examples.body:
Asexual reproduction is quick, needs no mate, and every offspring is a copy of a parent that was demonstrably good enough to survive. For a plant in a stable place that is an excellent bargain.

The catch arrives with the first new disease. If the clones are identical, a pathogen that can infect one can infect **all** of them, and there is no variation for anything to survive on. A banana plantation and a field of one potato variety are the same bet, and it is the bet sexual reproduction refuses to make.

visual.alt: A table setting asexual reproduction, with one parent, identical offspring and no cost, against sexual reproduction, which needs two parents and a mate but gives variation, so that some offspring survive a change

steps.title: Two ways of reproducing
steps.body:
**Asexual reproduction** involves **one parent**, and the offspring are **genetically identical** to that parent — clones. It uses **mitosis**.

**Sexual reproduction** involves **two parents**. Each contributes a **gamete** — a sex cell — and the two fuse at **fertilisation**. The offspring are **genetically different** from either parent and from each other.

**The specification asks for the advantages and disadvantages of each**, and lists them precisely.

**Asexual reproduction:**

- **Advantages**: no need to find a mate, and a rapid reproductive cycle.
- **Disadvantage**: no variation in the population.

**Sexual reproduction:**

- **Advantage**: variation in the population.
- **Disadvantage**: the requirement to find a mate.

**Notice that the two lists mirror each other.** What asexual reproduction gains in speed and convenience it loses in variation; what sexual reproduction gains in variation it pays for in the effort of finding a mate. Learning one list well gives you the other.

**Why variation matters so much** is the point behind all of this. A population of identical organisms is vulnerable: if conditions change, or a disease arrives that one of them cannot resist, **none** of them can resist it. A varied population is likely to contain **some** individuals that survive — which is the whole basis of natural selection.

steps.title: What meiosis does
steps.body:
**Meiotic cell division makes the gametes**, and the specification asks for its **role** — what it achieves — rather than how it happens.

**Three things to state:**

1. It produces **4 daughter cells**.
2. Each has **half the number of chromosomes** of the original cell.
3. This results in the formation of **genetically different haploid gametes**.

**The specification states plainly that the stages of meiosis are not required.** Prophase, metaphase and the rest are not examined here. What matters is the **outcome**.

**Haploid and diploid.** A cell with the **full** set of chromosomes is **diploid**; a human body cell is diploid with **46** chromosomes. A cell with **half** the set is **haploid**; a human gamete is haploid with **23**.

**Why halving is essential.** At fertilisation two gametes **fuse**. If each carried the full 46, the zygote would have 92 — and the number would double every generation. Halving first means $23 + 23 = 46$, and the chromosome number stays **constant** from one generation to the next.

**Why the gametes are genetically different.** The chromosomes are shared out differently into each of the four cells, so every gamete receives a **different combination**. This is the origin of the variation that sexual reproduction provides — and it is why siblings differ from one another.

steps.title: Meiosis against mitosis
steps.body:
**The two kinds of cell division do different jobs**, and confusing them is the commonest error in this part of the course.

**Mitosis** produces **2** daughter cells, each with the **full** number of chromosomes, and each **genetically identical** to the parent cell. It is used for **growth, repair and asexual reproduction**.

**Meiosis** produces **4** daughter cells, each with **half** the number of chromosomes, and each **genetically different**. It is used only to make **gametes**.

**Three differences, and they all point the same way.** Meiosis makes **more** cells, with **fewer** chromosomes, that are **less** alike. Mitosis makes **fewer** cells, with the **full** set, that are **identical**.

**Matching each to its purpose** explains why. Growth and repair need **exact copies** — a replacement skin cell must be a skin cell, with the full instructions. Reproduction needs **variation**, and needs the chromosome number **halved** so that fertilisation restores it rather than doubling it.

**A memory hook:** **mit**osis makes **mi**rror images; **mei**osis makes them **differ**. And the number of cells matches the number of letters difference — but the reliable way is to remember what each is **for**, because the purpose determines every one of the differences.

steps.title: Why variation is worth the cost
steps.body:
**Sexual reproduction is expensive.** A mate must be found, which takes time and energy and may fail. Asexual reproduction needs none of that and is far quicker. So why is sexual reproduction so widespread?

**The answer is variation, and what variation is worth when conditions change.**

**A population produced asexually is genetically identical.** If the environment changes — a new disease, a colder climate, a new predator — then whatever affects one individual affects **all of them in the same way**. If none can resist the disease, **none survives**.

**A population produced sexually is varied.** Some individuals will, by chance, happen to cope better than others. Those survive and reproduce, and the population **adapts**. This is the raw material that natural selection works on.

**So the trade is between the short term and the long term.** Asexual reproduction wins when conditions are **stable** and speed matters: a rapid cycle and no mate needed means numbers build very quickly. Sexual reproduction wins when conditions **change**, because the population can adapt.

**Many organisms use both.** Some plants spread asexually by runners when conditions suit them, and reproduce sexually by seed as well — taking the rapid cycle when it is safe and buying the variation as insurance.

**For the exam:** if a question describes a **changing** environment or a **disease**, the answer will involve **variation** and therefore sexual reproduction. If it stresses **speed** or **isolation**, asexual reproduction is likely to be favoured.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Give all three outcomes of meiosis.** **4 daughter cells**, each with **half the number of chromosomes**, resulting in **genetically different haploid gametes**. Answers that give one or two of the three are common and cost marks.

**Do not learn the stages.** The specification says **the stages of meiosis are not required**. Knowing what it **produces** is what is examined.

**Explain the halving through fertilisation.** Two gametes **fuse**, so if each had the full 46 the zygote would have 92 and the number would **double every generation**. Halving first keeps it **constant**. Saying "so the number stays the same" without the doubling argument is a weaker answer.

**Say why the gametes differ.** The chromosomes are **shared out differently** into each of the four cells, so each receives a **different combination**. That is the source of the variation sexual reproduction provides.

**Use the specification's own advantage and disadvantage lists.** Asexual: **no need to find a mate**, a **rapid reproductive cycle**, but **no variation in the population**. Sexual: **variation in the population**, but the **requirement to find a mate**. These are the phrases the mark scheme follows.

**Explain why variation is worth its cost.** In a **genetically identical** population, anything that harms one harms **all** — a new disease could wipe out the lot. In a varied population **some individuals may cope**, survive and reproduce. Variation is insurance against **change**, which is exactly why sexual reproduction persists despite being slower and harder.

**Keep mitosis and meiosis separate by purpose.** Growth and repair need **exact copies** with the full instructions, so **mitosis**. Reproduction needs **variation** and a **halved** chromosome number, so **meiosis**. Every difference between them follows from what each is for, which is more reliable than memorising a list.

**Watch the words haploid and diploid.** **Haploid** is half — a gamete. **Diploid** is the full set — a body cell or a zygote. Using them correctly is a quick signal of precision.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Asexual**: one parent, offspring **genetically identical**, uses **mitosis**.
- **Sexual**: two parents, gametes fuse, offspring **genetically different**.
- Asexual advantages: **no need to find a mate**, **a rapid reproductive cycle**.
- Asexual disadvantage: **no variation in the population**.
- Sexual advantage: **variation in the population**.
- Sexual disadvantage: **the requirement to find a mate**.
- **Meiosis** produces **4 daughter cells**.
- Each has **half the number of chromosomes**.
- The result is **genetically different haploid gametes**.
- **The stages of meiosis are not required.**
- **Haploid** = half the set (gamete, 23 in humans); **diploid** = full set (body cell, 46).
- Halving is needed because fertilisation **fuses two gametes** — otherwise the number would **double** each generation.
- Gametes differ because chromosomes are **shared out differently** into each.
- **Mitosis**: 2 cells, full number, **identical** — growth and repair.
- Variation matters because an **identical population cannot adapt** to change.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of meiosis, and explain why gametes must contain half the normal number of chromosomes.
questions.solution:
**Meiosis is the cell division that produces gametes**, and the specification asks for its **role** — what it achieves.

Meiosis produces **four daughter cells** from one original cell. Each of those cells has **half the number of chromosomes** of the original, and the result is the formation of **genetically different haploid gametes**. All three of those points matter: the number of cells, the halving, and the genetic difference between them.

It is worth noting that **the stages of meiosis are not required** by this specification — it is the outcome that is examined, not the mechanism.

**Haploid and diploid.** A cell containing the **full set** of chromosomes is **diploid**. A human body cell is diploid, with **46** chromosomes. A cell containing **half the set** is **haploid**, and a human gamete — a sperm or egg cell — is haploid with **23**.

**Why the gametes are genetically different** is that the chromosomes are **shared out differently** into each of the four daughter cells, so every gamete receives a **different combination**. This is the origin of the variation that sexual reproduction provides, and the reason siblings differ from one another despite having the same parents.

**Why the halving is necessary** becomes clear by following the chromosome number through **fertilisation**, which is the fusing of two gametes into a single zygote.

If each gamete carried the **full** 46 chromosomes, then fertilisation would produce a zygote with $46 + 46 = 92$. That offspring's own gametes would carry 92, giving grandchildren 184, and so on — the chromosome number would **double in every generation**, which is plainly impossible.

Because meiosis **halves** the number first, each gamete carries 23, and fertilisation restores the diploid number exactly: $23 + 23 = 46$. The chromosome number therefore stays **constant** from one generation to the next, however many generations pass.

So meiosis does two essential things at once. It **halves** the chromosome number, so that fertilisation restores rather than doubles it, and it produces cells that are **genetically different**, so that sexual reproduction generates the variation a population needs to adapt.

questions.prompt: Compare asexual and sexual reproduction, and explain why sexual reproduction is widespread despite its disadvantages.
questions.solution:
**Asexual reproduction** involves only **one parent**. The offspring are produced by **mitosis** and are therefore **genetically identical** to the parent and to each other — they are clones.

Its **advantages**, as the specification lists them, are that there is **no need to find a mate** and that there is a **rapid reproductive cycle**. Both are substantial: an organism can reproduce wherever it happens to be, without expending time or energy searching, and numbers can build extremely quickly.

Its **disadvantage** is that there is **no variation in the population**.

**Sexual reproduction** involves **two parents**. Each contributes a **haploid gamete**, produced by meiosis, and the two fuse at **fertilisation** to form a diploid zygote. Because meiosis shares the chromosomes out differently into each gamete, the offspring are **genetically different** from both parents and from each other.

Its **advantage** is **variation in the population**. Its **disadvantage** is the **requirement to find a mate**, which costs time and energy and may fail altogether.

Notice that the two lists are **mirror images**: what asexual reproduction gains in speed and convenience it loses in variation, and what sexual reproduction gains in variation it pays for in the difficulty of finding a partner.

**Why sexual reproduction persists despite these costs** comes down to what happens when **conditions change**.

In a population produced asexually, every individual is **genetically identical**. That means anything affecting one individual affects **all of them in exactly the same way**. If a new disease arrives and one plant cannot resist it, **none** of them can resist it, and the entire population may be destroyed. The same applies to a change in climate, a new predator, or a new pesticide.

In a population produced sexually, the individuals **vary**. When the same disease arrives, some individuals will — purely by chance — happen to have characteristics that let them survive. Those survive and **reproduce**, passing on the characteristics that helped them, and the population **adapts**. This is precisely the raw material that natural selection acts upon.

So the trade is between the **short term** and the **long term**. Asexual reproduction is better when conditions are **stable**: the rapid cycle and lack of a mate requirement let numbers build far faster. Sexual reproduction is better when conditions **change**, because it is the only one of the two that allows a population to respond.

A good illustration is a crop grown entirely from cuttings. It is quick and every plant is reliably identical, which suits a grower — until a disease arrives that the original plant could not resist, at which point the **whole crop** is lost at once. This is why many plants do **both**: spreading rapidly by runners when conditions allow, while also producing seed sexually, taking the immediate gain and buying the insurance at the same time.

So the trade is between the **short term** and the **long term**. Asexual reproduction is better when conditions are **stable**: the rapid cycle and lack of a mate requirement let numbers build far faster. Sexual reproduction is better when conditions **change**, because it is the only one of the two that allows a population to respond.

A good illustration is a crop grown entirely from cuttings. It is quick and every plant is reliably identical, which suits a grower — until a disease arrives that the original plant could not resist, at which point the **whole crop** is lost at once. This is why many plants do **both**: spreading rapidly by runners when conditions allow, while also producing seed sexually, taking the immediate gain and buying the insurance at the same time.

examTechnique.body:
Give **all three** outcomes of meiosis: **four cells**, **half the chromosomes**, **genetically different**. Do not learn the **stages** — the specification says they are not required.

Explain the halving through **fertilisation**: without it the number would **double** each generation. Use the specification's own advantage and disadvantage wording for the two kinds of reproduction.
examinerErrors: Giving only one or two of the three outcomes of meiosis.
Describing the stages of meiosis, which are not required.
Saying gametes are halved "so the number stays the same" without the doubling argument.
Inventing advantages instead of using the specification's list.
Saying variation is good without explaining what it protects against.
Forgetting that asexual reproduction uses mitosis.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives **all three** outcomes of meiosis and knows the **stages are not required**. It explains the halving by following fertilisation through — two gametes **fuse**, so without halving the number would **double every generation** — rather than merely asserting that it stays the same. It says **why** the gametes differ: the chromosomes are **shared out differently** into each. It uses the specification's own wording for advantages and disadvantages, and explains the value of variation concretely: an **identical** population meets a new disease with **no survivors**, while a varied one contains some that cope and can therefore **adapt**. It derives the mitosis/meiosis differences from **what each is for**.
